about: Groups is a 24-lecture Michaelmas Term course in Part IA of the Cambridge Mathematical Tripos and is the first course in abstract algebra. Following the official schedule it covers examples of groups (including symmetry groups and the Möbius group), Lagrange's theorem and small groups, group actions, quotient groups and the isomorphism theorem, matrix groups, and permutations, ending with the simplicity of A₅. It is examined on Paper 3 alongside Vector Calculus; each Part IA paper has a Section I of shorter questions and a Section II of longer ones.
topics: Small groups, quaternions and the Fermat–Euler theorem
Normal subgroups, quotient groups and the isomorphism theorem
Permutations, sign and the simplicity of A₅

notes.body:
Groups is the first abstract algebra course in Part IA. The schedule starts with the axioms and a stock of concrete examples, many of them geometric, because the rest of the course keeps coming back to them.

Definition
A group is a set G with a binary operation (g, h) ↦ gh such that:
- Closure: gh ∈ G for all g, h ∈ G.
- Associativity: (gh)k = g(hk).
- Identity: there is e ∈ G with eg = ge = g for all g.
- Inverses: each g has g⁻¹ with gg⁻¹ = g⁻¹g = e.
Simple consequences you should be able to prove in one line each: the identity is unique, inverses are unique, (gh)⁻¹ = h⁻¹g⁻¹, and cancellation holds (gh = gk implies h = k). The order of g is the least n ≥ 1 with gⁿ = e (or infinite if there is none). G is abelian if gh = hg for all g, h.

Standard examples
- (ℤ, +), (ℚ, +), (ℝ \ {0}, ×), and ℤₙ = integers mod n under addition.
- Cₙ, the cyclic group of order n, e.g. rotations of a regular n-gon.
- D₂ₙ, the dihedral group of all symmetries of a regular n-gon. Cambridge writes it with subscript 2n because it has 2n elements: n rotations and n reflections. With r a rotation by 2π/n and s a reflection, rⁿ = s² = e and srs = r⁻¹.
- Sₙ, the symmetric group of all bijections {1, …, n} → {1, …, n}, of order n!.
- Rotation groups of solids: the tetrahedron has 12 rotations and the cube has 24 (these counts are proved neatly with orbit–stabiliser later).
Non-examples: (ℤ, −) fails associativity; (ℤ \ {0}, ×) lacks inverses.

Subgroups
H ⊆ G is a subgroup (H ≤ G) if it is a group under the same operation. Subgroup test: H is non-empty and a, b ∈ H implies ab⁻¹ ∈ H. Examples: nℤ ≤ ℤ; the rotations form a subgroup of D₂ₙ; for any g, the cyclic subgroup ⟨g⟩ = {gⁿ : n ∈ ℤ}. Symmetry groups can be viewed as subgroups of permutation groups, by recording how each symmetry permutes the vertices.

Homomorphisms
A map φ: G → H is a homomorphism if φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b) for all a, b. Then φ(e) = e and φ(a⁻¹) = φ(a)⁻¹.
- ker φ = {g : φ(g) = e} is a subgroup of G; im φ is a subgroup of H.
- φ is injective if and only if ker φ = {e}. (If φ(a) = φ(b) then ab⁻¹ ∈ ker φ.)
- A bijective homomorphism is an isomorphism; G ≅ H means the groups are 'the same' abstractly.
Examples: det: GLₙ(ℝ) → ℝ \ {0}; the sign map Sₙ → {±1}; x ↦ eˣ from (ℝ, +) to (ℝ>0, ×), which is an isomorphism.

Cyclic groups
G is cyclic if G = ⟨g⟩ for some g. Every cyclic group is isomorphic to ℤ or to some Cₙ, and every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic (take the smallest positive power in the subgroup and use division with remainder). In Cₙ = ⟨g⟩, gᵏ has order n / gcd(n, k).

Direct products
G × H is the set of pairs with componentwise operation. For example C₂ × C₂ is the Klein four-group, which is not cyclic because every non-identity element has order 2. Also Cₘ × Cₙ ≅ Cₘₙ exactly when gcd(m, n) = 1.

Exam tips: Section I questions often ask you to check axioms or prove a short property (kernel is a subgroup, injective iff trivial kernel). State the subgroup test explicitly and verify non-emptiness.

The Möbius group is one of the distinctive examples in the Cambridge schedule: it links group theory with complex numbers and geometry, and it reappears in the matrix groups section.

Möbius maps
A Möbius map is f(z) = (az + b)/(cz + d) with a, b, c, d ∈ ℂ and ad − bc ≠ 0. It acts on the extended complex plane ℂ∞ = ℂ ∪ {∞}, with the conventions:
- if c ≠ 0: f(−d/c) = ∞ and f(∞) = a/c;
- if c = 0: f(∞) = ∞.
Each Möbius map is a bijection of ℂ∞, the inverse of f is z ↦ (dz − b)/(−cz + a), and composing two Möbius maps gives another, whose coefficients come from multiplying the 2×2 coefficient matrices. So the Möbius maps form a group M under composition. Multiplying a, b, c, d by the same non-zero λ gives the same map.

Building blocks
Every Möbius map is a composition of:
- translations z ↦ z + b,
- dilations and rotations z ↦ az (a ≠ 0),
- the inversion z ↦ 1/z.
For c ≠ 0 this follows from (az + b)/(cz + d) = a/c − (ad − bc)/(c(cz + d)).

Circles and lines
Call a circle or a straight line in ℂ a 'circle in ℂ∞' (a line passes through ∞). Möbius maps send circles in ℂ∞ to circles in ℂ∞. It suffices to check this for the building blocks; translations and dilations are clear, and z ↦ 1/z can be checked using the general equation Azz̄ + B̄z + Bz̄ + C = 0 (A, C real, B complex, |B|² > AC) for a circle (A ≠ 0) or line (A = 0).

Three points and the cross-ratio
Given three distinct points z₁, z₂, z₃ of ℂ∞ there is a unique Möbius map sending them to 0, 1, ∞, namely (for finite points)
f(z) = [(z − z₁)(z₂ − z₃)] / [(z − z₃)(z₂ − z₁)].
Hence Möbius maps act 'triply transitively': any three distinct points can be sent to any three distinct points, by exactly one map. The cross-ratio of four points can be defined as f(z₄) for this f. Conventions differ between books and lecturers (which of the points go to 0, 1, ∞); for example, some notes instead send z₁, z₂, z₃ to ∞, 0, 1 and evaluate at z₄. The different conventions give different numerical values for the same four points (related by permuting the points), so always state the one you use. The two key facts below hold in every convention. Key facts:
- The cross-ratio is invariant under Möbius maps: if g ∈ M, the four points g(zᵢ) have the same cross-ratio as the zᵢ.
- Four distinct points lie on a common circle in ℂ∞ if and only if their cross-ratio is real.

Conjugation and fixed points
Elements g, h are conjugate if h = kgk⁻¹ for some k; conjugate maps 'do the same thing in different coordinates'. A fixed point of f satisfies cz² + (d − a)z − b = 0 (with ∞ fixed when c = 0). So a non-identity Möbius map has one or two fixed points in ℂ∞. Consequently:
- with two fixed points, f is conjugate to z ↦ kz for some k ≠ 0, 1 (send the fixed points to 0 and ∞);
- with one fixed point, f is conjugate to z ↦ z + 1 (send the fixed point to ∞).
This makes iteration easy: if f = h⁻¹gh with g(z) = kz, then fⁿ = h⁻¹gⁿh and gⁿ(z) = kⁿz. If |k| < 1, every point other than the fixed point corresponding to ∞ is pulled towards the fixed point corresponding to 0 under iteration.

Worked example
f(z) = (2z + 1)/(z + 2). Fixed points: z(z + 2) = 2z + 1 gives z² = 1, so z = ±1. Let h(z) = (z − 1)/(z + 1), which sends 1 ↦ 0 and −1 ↦ ∞. Then h(f(z)) = (2z + 1 − z − 2)/(2z + 1 + z + 2) = (z − 1)/(3(z + 1)) = h(z)/3. So hfh⁻¹ is w ↦ w/3, and fⁿ(z) → 1 for every z ≠ −1.

Exam tips: always say how ∞ is handled, state your cross-ratio convention, and for fixed-point questions remember the case c = 0 (then ∞ is fixed).

Lagrange's theorem is the first big counting result of the course, and almost every later section uses it.

Cosets
Let H ≤ G. For g ∈ G the left coset is gH = {gh : h ∈ H} and the right coset is Hg = {hg : h ∈ H}.
Key facts (prove them):
- g ∈ gH, since e ∈ H.
- aH = bH if and only if b⁻¹a ∈ H.
- Two left cosets are either equal or disjoint. If x ∈ aH ∩ bH then x = ah₁ = bh₂, so a = bh₂h₁⁻¹ ∈ bH and hence aH ⊆ bH; by symmetry aH = bH.
- Every left coset has |H| elements, because h ↦ gh is a bijection H → gH (its inverse is multiplication by g⁻¹).
So the left cosets partition G into blocks of equal size.

Lagrange's theorem
If G is finite and H ≤ G then |H| divides |G|. The number of left cosets is the index |G : H| = |G|/|H|.

Corollaries
- The order of any element g divides |G|, since ⟨g⟩ is a subgroup of order equal to the order of g.
- g^|G| = e for every g ∈ G.
- A group of prime order p is cyclic, and every non-identity element generates it (its order divides p and is not 1).
- If |G| = p is prime, the only subgroups are {e} and G.

The converse is false
Lagrange says subgroup orders divide |G|, not that every divisor occurs. The standard counterexample is A₄, of order 12, which has no subgroup of order 6. (If H had order 6 it would have index 2, so g² ∈ H for every g, because the quotient has order 2. Each 3-cycle σ satisfies σ = σ⁴ = (σ²)², so σ ∈ H. That puts all eight 3-cycles in H, which is too many for a group of order 6.) By contrast, Cauchy's theorem (later) guarantees elements, and hence subgroups, of every prime order dividing |G|.

Left versus right cosets
They can differ. In S₃ (composing right to left) take H = {e, (1 2)}. Then
- (1 3)H = {(1 3), (1 3)(1 2)} = {(1 3), (1 2 3)},
- H(1 3) = {(1 3), (1 2)(1 3)} = {(1 3), (1 3 2)}.
These differ, which is exactly why H is not normal in S₃. When gH = Hg for all g, H is normal, and the cosets form the quotient group (see the quotient groups topic).

Worked example
G = D₁₂ (order 12). Possible subgroup orders are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The rotation subgroup ⟨r⟩ ≅ C₆ has index 2, so its two cosets are the rotations and the reflections. An element of order 5 cannot exist because 5 does not divide 12.

Proof structure to learn
1. Define cosets; show they cover G (g ∈ gH).
2. Show any two are equal or disjoint.
3. Show all have size |H|.
4. Conclude |G| = (number of cosets) × |H|.
Section I questions often ask for exactly this, and the marks are in steps 2 and 3.

Exam tips: be explicit that the map h ↦ gh is a bijection (injective by cancellation, surjective by definition). When applying Lagrange, check whether the question needs an element of a given order (use Cauchy) or just a divisibility restriction.

notes.h: Small groups, quaternions and the Fermat–Euler theorem
notes.body:
This part of the schedule uses Lagrange's theorem to classify groups of small order and to prove a classical number-theory result.

Groups of order up to 8 (up to isomorphism)
- Order 1: the trivial group.
- Orders 2, 3, 5, 7 (primes): only the cyclic group, by Lagrange.
- Order 4: C₄ and C₂ × C₂ (the Klein four-group). If there is an element of order 4 the group is cyclic; otherwise all three non-identity elements have order 2.
- Order 6: C₆ and D₆ (≅ S₃).
- Order 8: five groups: C₈, C₄ × C₂, C₂ × C₂ × C₂, D₈ and the quaternion group Q₈.

Useful lemmas for classification
- If every non-identity element has order 2 then G is abelian: ab = (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ = ba.
- If G has an element whose order equals |G|, G is cyclic.
- For order 6 without an element of order 6: not every element can have order 2 (an abelian group of order 6 with all elements of order 2 would contain a Klein four-group, and 4 does not divide 6), so there is an element a of order 3. Take b ∉ ⟨a⟩; considering where b² and bab⁻¹ lie forces b² = e and bab⁻¹ = a⁻¹, giving D₆.

The quaternion group Q₈
Q₈ = {±1, ±i, ±j, ±k} with i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1. From these: ij = k, jk = i, ki = j, and ji = −k, kj = −i, ik = −j. Properties:
- It is non-abelian (ij ≠ ji).
- −1 is its only element of order 2; the other six non-identity elements ±i, ±j, ±k have order 4.
- Every subgroup is normal, even though Q₈ is not abelian.
- It can be realised by 2×2 complex matrices, e.g. i ↦ [[i, 0], [0, −i]] and j ↦ [[0, 1], [−1, 0]].
Distinguishing D₈ from Q₈: D₈ has five elements of order 2 (four reflections and r²) and two of order 4, while Q₈ has one of order 2 and six of order 4. Counting element orders is the standard way to show groups are not isomorphic.

The Fermat–Euler theorem
Let n ≥ 2 and let Uₙ = (ℤ/nℤ)^× be the set of residues a mod n with gcd(a, n) = 1. Under multiplication mod n it is a group: closure holds since a product of numbers coprime to n is coprime to n, and inverses exist by Bezout (if ax + ny = 1 then ax ≡ 1 mod n). Its order is Euler's totient φ(n).
- Euler's theorem: if gcd(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n). Proof: Lagrange gives that the order of a in Uₙ divides φ(n).
- Fermat's little theorem: if p is prime and p ∤ a then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p), since φ(p) = p − 1.

Worked examples
- 3¹⁰⁰ mod 7: 3⁶ ≡ 1, and 100 = 6 × 16 + 4, so 3¹⁰⁰ ≡ 3⁴ = 81 ≡ 4 (mod 7).
- Last digit of 7²²²: φ(10) = 4 and 222 = 4 × 55 + 2, so 7²²² ≡ 7² = 49 ≡ 9 (mod 10). The last digit is 9.
- φ(12) = 4, with U₁₂ = {1, 5, 7, 11}; every element squares to 1, so U₁₂ ≅ C₂ × C₂ rather than C₄.

Exam tips: when asked to list groups of order 8, give all five and a one-line reason why no two are isomorphic (abelian or not, and numbers of elements of each order). For Fermat–Euler, say explicitly which group you apply Lagrange to.

Group actions turn abstract groups into symmetries of something concrete, and the orbit–stabiliser theorem is the main counting tool of the course.

Definition
An action of G on a set X is a map G × X → X, (g, x) ↦ g·x, with
- e·x = x for all x, and
- g·(h·x) = (gh)·x for all g, h, x.
Equivalently, an action is a homomorphism ρ: G → Sym(X), where ρ(g) is the permutation x ↦ g·x. The action is faithful if ker ρ = {e}.

Orbits and stabilisers
- Orbit of x: Orb(x) = {g·x : g ∈ G}. Orbits partition X.
- Stabiliser of x: Stab(x) = {g : g·x = x}, a subgroup of G.
- The action is transitive if there is only one orbit.

Orbit–stabiliser theorem
For finite G, |G| = |Orb(x)| × |Stab(x)|. Proof: the map from left cosets of Stab(x) to Orb(x), g Stab(x) ↦ g·x, is well defined and injective, because g·x = h·x ⇔ h⁻¹g ∈ Stab(x) ⇔ g Stab(x) = h Stab(x); it is clearly surjective. So |Orb(x)| = |G : Stab(x)|, and Lagrange finishes.

Applications to symmetry groups
- Rotations of a cube: the group acts transitively on the 6 faces; the rotations fixing a face are the 4 rotations about the axis through its centre. So the group has 6 × 4 = 24 elements.
- Rotations of a regular tetrahedron: transitive on 4 vertices, stabiliser of a vertex has 3 elements, so 12 rotations.
- Acting on the 4 long diagonals of a cube gives an isomorphism from the cube's rotation group to S₄.

Cayley's theorem
Every group is isomorphic to a subgroup of a symmetric group. G acts on itself by left multiplication, g·x = gx. This action is faithful (if gx = x for all x then g = e), so G embeds in Sym(G); if |G| = n this is Sₙ.

Conjugation
G acts on itself by conjugation: g·x = gxg⁻¹.
- Orbits are conjugacy classes ccl(x).
- The stabiliser of x is the centraliser C(x) = {g : gx = xg}.
- So |ccl(x)| = |G|/|C(x)| divides |G|.
- The centre Z(G) = {x : xg = gx for all g} is the set of elements whose class has size 1.
The class equation |G| = Σ |ccl(x)| (one x per class) is useful in counting.

Cauchy's theorem
If p is a prime dividing |G|, then G has an element of order p. A standard proof: let X = {(g₁, …, gₚ) ∈ Gᵖ : g₁g₂⋯gₚ = e}. Choosing g₁, …, gₚ₋₁ freely determines gₚ, so |X| = |G|^(p−1), divisible by p. The cyclic group Cₚ acts on X by cyclically shifting entries; this preserves X because g₂⋯gₚg₁ = g₁⁻¹(g₁⋯gₚ)g₁ = e. Orbits have size 1 or p (orbit–stabiliser in Cₚ). Fixed points are the tuples (g, …, g) with gᵖ = e. Since p divides |X| and every non-fixed point lies in an orbit of size p, p divides the number of fixed points. (e, …, e) is one, so there are at least p of them, giving some g ≠ e with gᵖ = e, which has order p.

Exam tips: in orbit–stabiliser questions, name the set being acted on, show transitivity, and identify the stabiliser explicitly. Cauchy's theorem proofs are popular in Section II; learn the action on p-tuples carefully, especially why the shift preserves X.

notes.h: Normal subgroups, quotient groups and the isomorphism theorem
notes.body:
This section explains when cosets can themselves be multiplied, and it gives the isomorphism theorem, which is the main tool for identifying quotient groups.

Normal subgroups
A subgroup K ≤ G is normal (K ◁ G) if gKg⁻¹ = K for all g ∈ G. Equivalent conditions:
- gkg⁻¹ ∈ K for all g ∈ G, k ∈ K;
- gK = Kg for all g (left cosets equal right cosets);
- K is a union of conjugacy classes of G.
Examples:
- Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal.
- Every kernel of a homomorphism is normal: if φ(k) = e then φ(gkg⁻¹) = φ(g)φ(g)⁻¹ = e.
- Any subgroup of index 2 is normal (the two left cosets are K and G \ K, and so are the two right cosets).
- Aₙ ◁ Sₙ, SLₙ(ℝ) ◁ GLₙ(ℝ), and the rotations form a normal subgroup of D₂ₙ.
Non-example: {e, (1 2)} is not normal in S₃, since (1 3)(1 2)(1 3) = (2 3).
Normality is not transitive. With V = {e, (1 2)(3 4), (1 3)(2 4), (1 4)(2 3)}: K = {e, (1 2)(3 4)} ◁ V (V is abelian) and V ◁ S₄, but K is not normal in S₄, as conjugating (1 2)(3 4) gives the other double transpositions.

Quotient groups
If K ◁ G, the set G/K of cosets is a group under (aK)(bK) = abK. The point is well-definedness: if aK = a'K and bK = b'K, then a' = ak₁ and b' = bk₂ for some k₁, k₂ ∈ K, and
a'b' = ak₁bk₂ = ab(b⁻¹k₁b)k₂ ∈ abK,
because b⁻¹k₁b ∈ K by normality. The identity is K and the inverse of aK is a⁻¹K. Also |G/K| = |G|/|K|.
Examples: ℤ/nℤ ≅ Cₙ; Sₙ/Aₙ ≅ C₂; D₂ₙ/⟨r⟩ ≅ C₂.

The isomorphism theorem
If φ: G → H is a homomorphism, then ker φ ◁ G and
G/ker φ ≅ im φ, via g ker φ ↦ φ(g).
Proof outline: the map θ(g ker φ) = φ(g) is well defined and injective because g ker φ = h ker φ ⇔ h⁻¹g ∈ ker φ ⇔ φ(h) = φ(g). It is a homomorphism since θ(gK hK) = φ(gh) = φ(g)φ(h), and it is onto im φ by definition.

Standard applications
- det: GLₙ(ℝ) → ℝ \ {0} is a surjective homomorphism with kernel SLₙ(ℝ), so GLₙ(ℝ)/SLₙ(ℝ) ≅ (ℝ \ {0}, ×).
- θ: (ℝ, +) → S¹ = {z ∈ ℂ : |z| = 1}, x ↦ e^(2πix), is surjective with kernel ℤ, so ℝ/ℤ ≅ S¹.
- sgn: Sₙ → {±1} (n ≥ 2) is surjective with kernel Aₙ, so |Aₙ| = n!/2.
- ℤ → ℤₙ, reduction mod n, gives ℤ/nℤ ≅ ℤₙ.
- The map GL₂(ℂ) → Möbius group has kernel the non-zero scalar matrices (see matrix groups).

Recipe for 'identify G/K' questions
1. Find a homomorphism out of G whose kernel is exactly K.
2. Show it is surjective onto a group you recognise (or compute its image).
3. Quote the isomorphism theorem.
Checking the kernel carefully (both inclusions) is where marks are lost.

Exam tips: always prove well-definedness when constructing a quotient or a map out of one. 'Show K is normal' is often easiest by exhibiting K as a kernel.

The schedule's matrix groups section is short (three lectures) but connects the course to Vectors and Matrices and to the Möbius group.

The general and special linear groups
- GLₙ(F) is the group of invertible n×n matrices over F (F = ℝ or ℂ) under multiplication.
- SLₙ(F) = {A : det A = 1}. Since det(AB) = det A det B, det is a homomorphism GLₙ(F) → F \ {0}, and SLₙ(F) is its kernel, hence a normal subgroup. det is surjective, so GLₙ(F)/SLₙ(F) ≅ F \ {0}.

Link with the Möbius group
Send A = [[a, b], [c, d]] ∈ GL₂(ℂ) to the Möbius map f_A(z) = (az + b)/(cz + d). Then f_(AB) = f_A ∘ f_B, so this is a surjective homomorphism GL₂(ℂ) → M. Its kernel is the set of A with f_A = identity, which is exactly the non-zero scalar matrices λI. So M ≅ GL₂(ℂ)/{λI : λ ≠ 0}. Restricting to SL₂(ℂ) (every Möbius map can be scaled so ad − bc = 1), the kernel becomes {I, −I}, so M ≅ SL₂(ℂ)/{±I}.

Orthogonal groups
- O(n) = {A ∈ GLₙ(ℝ) : AᵀA = I}. These are exactly the matrices preserving the dot product (Ax·Ay = x·y), hence lengths and angles.
- det A = ±1 for A ∈ O(n), since det(AᵀA) = (det A)² = 1.
- SO(n) = {A ∈ O(n) : det A = 1} is the kernel of det on O(n), a normal subgroup of index 2.

The case n = 2
- Rotations: R(θ) = [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]], which form SO(2) ≅ S¹.
- Reflections: [[cos θ, sin θ], [sin θ, −cos θ]], reflection in the line through 0 at angle θ/2 to the x-axis.
O(2) is the union of these two families.

The case n = 3
- Every A ∈ SO(3) has an axis. Proof: det(A − I) = det(A − AAᵀ) = det A · det(I − Aᵀ) = det(I − A) = (−1)³ det(A − I), so det(A − I) = 0. Thus 1 is an eigenvalue, and A fixes a line (the axis). A preserves the plane perpendicular to the axis and acts there as a rotation.
- Reflection in the plane through 0 with unit normal n is x ↦ x − 2(x·n)n; it has determinant −1.
- Every element of O(3) is a product of at most three reflections, and every rotation is a product of two (reflections in two planes containing the axis, at half the rotation angle).

Change of basis as conjugation
If a linear map has matrix A in one basis and P is the change-of-basis matrix, its matrix in the new basis is P⁻¹AP. So conjugate matrices represent the same linear map in different coordinates. In SO(3), a rotation through θ about one axis is conjugate to the rotation through θ about any other axis: conjugate by a rotation taking one axis to the other. This mirrors the Möbius conjugacy results in the first section.

Exam tips: be fluent with the 2×2 rotation and reflection matrices and with the proof that rotations of ℝ³ have an axis. When asked about the Möbius group as a quotient, state the homomorphism and compute its kernel carefully, including why only scalar matrices act trivially.

notes.h: Permutations, sign and the simplicity of A₅
notes.body:
The final section returns to Sₙ in detail and ends with one of the course's showpiece results: A₅ is simple.

Cycle notation
Every permutation can be written as a product of disjoint cycles, uniquely up to the order of the cycles (and the starting point within each cycle). Disjoint cycles commute. The order of a permutation is the lcm of its cycle lengths: (1 2 3)(4 5) has order lcm(3, 2) = 6. The cycle type lists the cycle lengths.

Composition convention
Cambridge courses usually compose right to left, as for functions: στ means 'do τ first'. Example: (1 2 3)(1 2) sends 1 → 2 → 3, 2 → 1 → 2, 3 → 3 → 1, giving (1 3). Always check which convention a question uses.

Transpositions and sign
- Every permutation is a product of transpositions: (a₁ a₂ … aₖ) = (a₁ aₖ)(a₁ aₖ₋₁)⋯(a₁ a₂), so a k-cycle is a product of k − 1 transpositions.
- The parity theorem: the number of transpositions in such an expression is always even or always odd for a given permutation. One proof counts how a transposition changes the number of cycles (by exactly ±1) in the disjoint cycle decomposition, including 1-cycles.
- So sgn: Sₙ → {±1} is a well-defined homomorphism, with sgn(transposition) = −1 and sgn(k-cycle) = (−1)^(k−1).
- Aₙ = ker sgn is the alternating group; for n ≥ 2 it has index 2 and order n!/2.

Conjugacy in Sₙ
If τ = (a₁ a₂ … aₖ)⋯ then στσ⁻¹ = (σ(a₁) σ(a₂) … σ(aₖ))⋯: just relabel the entries. Hence two permutations are conjugate in Sₙ if and only if they have the same cycle type. For S₄ the classes are: identity (1), transpositions (6), double transpositions (3), 3-cycles (8), 4-cycles (6), totalling 24.

Conjugacy in Aₙ
An Sₙ-class contained in Aₙ either stays a single Aₙ-class or splits into two classes of equal size. It splits exactly when no odd permutation commutes with σ, i.e. when C_Sₙ(σ) ⊆ Aₙ. A useful criterion: the class splits if and only if the cycle type consists of distinct odd lengths (counting fixed points as 1-cycles).
- A₄: 1 + 3 + 4 + 4 (the eight 3-cycles split). Since {e} ∪ {double transpositions} is a normal subgroup of order 4, A₄ is not simple.
- A₅: identity 1; double transpositions 15; 3-cycles 20 (no split, as the type 3, 1, 1 repeats 1); 5-cycles 24 split as 12 + 12. Total 1 + 15 + 20 + 12 + 12 = 60.

Simple groups and A₅
G is simple if its only normal subgroups are {e} and G. Cₚ (p prime) is simple. A normal subgroup is a union of conjugacy classes that includes {e}, and its order divides |G|. For A₅ the possible sums containing 1 are 1, 13, 16, 21, 25, 28, 33, 36, 40, 45, 48 and 60; the only ones dividing 60 are 1 and 60. So A₅ is simple; it is the smallest non-abelian simple group.

Worked example
How many elements of S₆ have cycle type (3, 3)? Choose and arrange: 6!/(3² × 2!) = 720/18 = 40. In general the class with mᵢ cycles of length i has n!/∏(i^mᵢ · mᵢ!) elements.

Exam tips: show the class sizes in A₅ with a short justification for each (e.g. why the 5-cycles split: the centraliser of a 5-cycle in S₅ is the cyclic group it generates, which lies in A₅). State the composition convention before computing products.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a group?
questions.why: Subtraction is not associative: (1 − 2) − 3 = −4 but 1 − (2 − 3) = 2, so (ℤ, −) is not a group. (ℤ, +) and (ℚ \ {0}, ×) are standard groups, and {1, −1, i, −i} is the cyclic group of order 4 under multiplication.

questions.q: How many elements of order 2 are there in D₈, the symmetry group of a square?
questions.why: The four reflections each have order 2, and so does the half-turn r². That gives 5. '1' counts only the half-turn, '4' only the reflections; the quarter-turns r and r³ have order 4, so 6 is too many.

questions.q: Let φ: G → H be a group homomorphism. Prove that φ is injective if and only if ker φ = {e}.
markScheme: Shows φ(e) = e so e ∈ ker φ; injective implies only e maps to e
Conversely assumes ker φ = {e} and φ(a) = φ(b)
Deduces φ(ab⁻¹) = φ(a)φ(b)⁻¹ = e, using φ(b⁻¹) = φ(b)⁻¹
Concludes ab⁻¹ = e so a = b
questions.modelAnswer: First φ(e) = φ(ee) = φ(e)φ(e), so cancelling gives φ(e) = e, and e ∈ ker φ. If φ is injective, any g with φ(g) = e = φ(e) must equal e, so ker φ = {e}. Conversely suppose ker φ = {e} and φ(a) = φ(b). Since φ(b)φ(b⁻¹) = φ(bb⁻¹) = e, we have φ(b⁻¹) = φ(b)⁻¹. Then φ(ab⁻¹) = φ(a)φ(b)⁻¹ = e, so ab⁻¹ ∈ ker φ = {e}, giving ab⁻¹ = e and a = b. Hence φ is injective.

questions.q: What are the fixed points in ℂ∞ of f(z) = (3z − 2)/(z)?
questions.why: Solve z = (3z − 2)/z, i.e. z² − 3z + 2 = 0, so z = 1 or 2. ∞ is not fixed because c = 1 ≠ 0 gives f(∞) = 3, and f(0) = ∞, so 0 is not fixed. −1, −2 come from a sign slip, and the quadratic has two distinct roots, not one.

questions.q: The non-identity Möbius map f(z) = z/(z + 1) has exactly one fixed point. To which map is it conjugate?
questions.why: Fixed points: z(z + 1) = z gives z² = 0, so 0 is the only fixed point (∞ ↦ 1). A non-identity map with exactly one fixed point is conjugate to a translation z ↦ z + 1. The other options each have two fixed points (0 and ∞ for 2z and −z; ±1 for 1/z).

questions.q: Find the Möbius map f with f(0) = 1, f(1) = ∞ and f(∞) = −1. Find its fixed points.
markScheme: Uses f(1) = ∞ to put a factor (z − 1) in the denominator
Uses f(∞) = −1 to fix ratio a/c = −1
Uses f(0) = 1 to find b/d and obtains f(z) = (z + 1)/(1 − z) (or equivalent)
Fixed points ±i
questions.modelAnswer: f(1) = ∞ means the denominator vanishes at z = 1, so take f(z) = (az + b)/(z − 1) up to scaling (c = 1, d = −1). f(∞) = a/c = a = −1. f(0) = b/(−1) = 1 gives b = −1. So f(z) = (−z − 1)/(z − 1) = (z + 1)/(1 − z), with ad − bc = (−1)(−1) − (−1)(1) = 2 ≠ 0. Fixed points: z(1 − z) = z + 1, so z − z² = z + 1, i.e. z² = −1, giving z = i and z = −i. (∞ is not fixed as f(∞) = −1.)

questions.q: A group G has order 35. Which of the following could NOT be the order of an element of G?
questions.why: By Lagrange, element orders divide |G| = 35, so the possible orders are 1, 5, 7 and 35. 10 does not divide 35. The identity has order 1, and 5 and 7 are divisors of 35.

questions.q: Let H = {e, (1 2)} in S₃ (composition right to left). Which statement is true?
options: H is the kernel of the sign homomorphism
questions.why: (1 3)(1 2) sends 1 → 2, 2 → 3, 3 → 1, so it is (1 2 3); (1 2)(1 3) is (1 3 2). So left and right cosets differ, and the claim (1 3)H = H(1 3) is false. H does not have index 2: |S₃ : H| = 6/2 = 3. H is not the kernel of sign either: that kernel is A₃ = {e, (1 2 3), (1 3 2)}, of order 3.

questions.q: State and prove Lagrange's theorem.
markScheme: Correct statement: finite G, H ≤ G implies |H| divides |G|
Every g lies in a left coset (g = ge ∈ gH)
Proof that two left cosets are equal or disjoint
Proof that |gH| = |H| via the bijection h ↦ gh
Conclusion |G| = k|H| where k is the number of distinct cosets
questions.modelAnswer: Statement: if G is a finite group and H ≤ G then |H| divides |G|. Proof: each g ∈ G lies in the left coset gH since g = ge and e ∈ H, so the left cosets cover G. If aH and bH share an element x = ah₁ = bh₂, then a = bh₂h₁⁻¹, so for any h ∈ H, ah = b(h₂h₁⁻¹h) ∈ bH, giving aH ⊆ bH; by symmetry aH = bH. So distinct cosets are disjoint. The map H → gH, h ↦ gh, is surjective by definition and injective since gh = gh' implies h = h' by cancellation, so |gH| = |H|. Hence G is a disjoint union of k cosets each of size |H|, and |G| = k|H|.

questions.q: What is 3¹⁰⁰ mod 7?
questions.why: By Fermat, 3⁶ ≡ 1 mod 7. 100 = 96 + 4, so 3¹⁰⁰ ≡ 3⁴ = 81 = 77 + 4 ≡ 4. Answer 1 misapplies Fermat as if 3ⁿ ≡ 1 for any large n; it would need 6 to divide 100. Answer 3 is 3¹ and answer 5 is 3⁵ mod 7 (3⁵ = 243 = 34 × 7 + 5), which arise from taking the remainder of 100 on division by 6 wrongly (it is 4, not 1 or 5).

questions.q: Which group of order 8 has exactly one element of order 2?
questions.why: In Q₈ only −1 has order 2; ±i, ±j, ±k have order 4. D₈ has five elements of order 2, C₂ × C₂ × C₂ has seven, and C₄ × C₂ has three ((2,0), (0,1), (2,1) in additive notation).

questions.q: Define the group Uₙ of units modulo n and use Lagrange's theorem to prove that a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) whenever gcd(a, n) = 1. Hence find the last digit of 7²²².
markScheme: Uₙ = residues mod n coprime to n under multiplication mod n, order φ(n)
Checks closure and existence of inverses (Bezout)
Order of a divides |Uₙ| = φ(n) by Lagrange, so a^φ(n) ≡ 1
Last digit 9
questions.modelAnswer: Uₙ is the set of residue classes a mod n with gcd(a, n) = 1, under multiplication mod n. It is closed because a product of integers coprime to n is coprime to n; multiplication is associative; 1 is the identity; and if gcd(a, n) = 1, Bezout gives x, y with ax + ny = 1, so x is an inverse of a mod n (and x is coprime to n). So Uₙ is a group of order φ(n). If gcd(a, n) = 1, a lies in Uₙ; by Lagrange its order d divides φ(n), so a^φ(n) = (a^d)^(φ(n)/d) ≡ 1. For 7²²²: φ(10) = 4 and 222 = 4 × 55 + 2, so 7²²² ≡ 7² = 49 ≡ 9 mod 10. The last digit is 9.

questions.q: The full symmetry group (rotations and reflections) of a regular tetrahedron acts transitively on its 4 vertices. The stabiliser of a vertex is isomorphic to S₃. What is the order of the group?
questions.why: Orbit–stabiliser: 4 × |S₃| = 4 × 6 = 24 (in fact the group is S₄). 12 is the rotation group only (stabiliser C₃). 10 adds the orbit size and the stabiliser order (4 + 6) instead of multiplying them. 48 doubles 24 to 'include the reflections', but the S₃ stabiliser already contains the reflections fixing the vertex, so nothing is missing (48 is in fact the order of the cube's full symmetry group).

questions.q: In a group of order 15, which statement must be true?
options: G has elements of order 3 and of order 5
G has an element of order 2
G has a subgroup of order 6
questions.why: Cauchy's theorem gives elements of each prime order dividing 15, i.e. 3 and 5. Order 2 is impossible since 2 does not divide 15, and a subgroup of order 6 is impossible by Lagrange since 6 does not divide 15. Being non-abelian is false: C₁₅ is an abelian group of order 15 (in fact every group of order 15 is cyclic, though proving that needs theory beyond this course).

questions.q: Using the orbit–stabiliser theorem, show that the group G of rotations of a cube has order 24, and identify the stabiliser of a vertex.
markScheme: Identifies a set G acts on transitively (faces or vertices)
Justifies transitivity (rotations move any face/vertex to any other)
Identifies the stabiliser (4 rotations about a face axis, or 3 about a diagonal)
Applies |G| = |Orb| × |Stab| to get 24
Vertex stabiliser is cyclic of order 3 (rotations about the long diagonal), consistent with 8 × 3 = 24
questions.modelAnswer: G acts on the 6 faces. Rotations by π/2 about the axes through opposite face centres, and their composites, can move any face to any other, so the action is transitive and the orbit has size 6. The stabiliser of the top face consists of rotations mapping the top face to itself; these are the rotations about the vertical axis through 0, π/2, π, 3π/2, so it has order 4. Hence |G| = 6 × 4 = 24. G also acts transitively on the 8 vertices; a rotation fixing a vertex must fix the opposite vertex too (it preserves the centre), so it is a rotation about that long diagonal, and the three rotations through 0, 2π/3, 4π/3 all preserve the cube. So the vertex stabiliser is cyclic of order 3, and indeed 8 × 3 = 24.

questions.q: Which subgroup is NOT normal in the given group?
questions.why: (1 3)(1 2)(1 3) = (2 3) ∉ {e, (1 2)}, so it is not normal. A₃ and ⟨r⟩ have index 2, hence are normal, and SL₂(ℝ) is the kernel of det, hence normal.

questions.q: Using φ: (ℂ \ {0}, ×) → (ℝ>0, ×), z ↦ |z|, the isomorphism theorem shows that the circle group S¹ = {|z| = 1} is normal and that ℂ \ {0} modulo S¹ is isomorphic to:
questions.why: |zw| = |z||w| so φ is a homomorphism; it is surjective onto ℝ>0 and its kernel is S¹. Hence (ℂ \ {0})/S¹ ≅ (ℝ>0, ×) (which is itself isomorphic to (ℝ, +) via log). (ℤ, +) and (ℚ>0, ×) are countable, so they cannot be isomorphic to the uncountable group ℝ>0. S¹ is not isomorphic to it either: S¹ contains −1, of order 2, whereas the only element of finite order in (ℝ>0, ×) is 1.

questions.q: Let K ◁ G. Show that the rule (aK)(bK) = abK gives a well-defined group operation on G/K. Give an example showing the rule can fail to be well defined if K is not normal.
markScheme: Takes a' ∈ aK, b' ∈ bK, writes a' = ak₁, b' = bk₂
Shows a'b' = ab(b⁻¹k₁b)k₂ and uses normality to get a'b'K = abK
Checks associativity, identity K, inverse a⁻¹K
Counterexample: K = {e, (1 2)} in S₃ with explicit cosets
Shows two representatives of the same cosets give different product cosets
questions.modelAnswer: Suppose aK = a'K and bK = b'K, so a' = ak₁ and b' = bk₂ with k₁, k₂ ∈ K. Then a'b' = ak₁bk₂ = ab(b⁻¹k₁b)k₂. Since K is normal, b⁻¹k₁b ∈ K, so a'b' ∈ abK and a'b'K = abK: the product does not depend on representatives. Associativity is inherited: (aK bK)cK = (ab)cK = a(bc)K. K = eK is the identity and a⁻¹K is the inverse of aK. So G/K is a group. Counterexample: in S₃ let K = {e, (1 2)}. Then (1 3)K = (1 2 3)K since (1 2 3) = (1 3)(1 2). Multiply each by (1 3)K: (1 3)(1 3)K = K, but (1 2 3)(1 3) = (2 3) (check: 1 → 3 → 1, 2 → 2 → 3, 3 → 1 → 2), and (2 3)K = {(2 3), (2 3)(1 2)} ≠ K. So the 'product' depends on the representative.

questions.q: What is the kernel of the homomorphism SL₂(ℂ) → M (Möbius group), A ↦ f_A?
options: All scalar matrices λI with λ ≠ 0
questions.why: f_A is the identity only for scalar A = λI; within SL₂(ℂ), det(λI) = λ² = 1 forces λ = ±1. {I} misses −I, which also gives z ↦ z. All scalars is the kernel on GL₂(ℂ), not SL₂(ℂ). SO(2) contains non-trivial rotations which give non-identity Möbius maps.

questions.q: Which of these matrices lies in O(2) but not SO(2)?
questions.why: [[1, 0], [0, −1]] is reflection in the x-axis: orthogonal with determinant −1. [[0, −1], [1, 0]] is rotation by π/2 (det 1, in SO(2)). [[2, 0], [0, ½]] and [[1, 1], [0, 1]] have determinant 1 but are not orthogonal (they change lengths, e.g. the first sends (1, 0) to (2, 0) and the shear sends (0, 1) to (1, 1)), so they are in SL₂(ℝ) but not O(2).

questions.q: Prove that every A ∈ SO(3) fixes a non-zero vector, and explain why A then acts as a rotation of the plane perpendicular to it.
markScheme: Uses AAᵀ = I to write A − I = A(I − Aᵀ)
Takes determinants: det(A − I) = det(I − A)
Uses n = 3 odd: det(I − A) = −det(A − I), so det(A − I) = 0
Concludes 1 is an eigenvalue with eigenvector v ≠ 0
Orthogonality: x·v = 0 implies Ax·v = Ax·Av = x·v = 0; restriction is orthogonal with det 1, so a rotation
questions.modelAnswer: Since AᵀA = AAᵀ = I, A − I = A − AAᵀ = A(I − Aᵀ). Taking determinants, det(A − I) = det A · det((I − A)ᵀ) = 1 · det(I − A). For a 3×3 matrix, det(I − A) = det(−(A − I)) = (−1)³ det(A − I) = −det(A − I). So det(A − I) = −det(A − I), giving det(A − I) = 0. Hence there is v ≠ 0 with Av = v. Let P = {x : x·v = 0}. If x ∈ P then Ax·v = Ax·Av = x·v = 0, so A maps P to itself. Take an orthonormal basis u = v/|v|, e₂, e₃ of ℝ³ with e₂, e₃ spanning P. In this basis A has block form diag(1, B), where B is the 2×2 matrix of A restricted to P. B preserves lengths, so it is orthogonal, and det B = det A = 1. An orthogonal map of a plane with determinant 1 is a rotation, so A is a rotation about the axis spanned by v.

questions.q: What is the sign of the permutation (1 2 3 4)(5 6 7) in S₇?
options: It depends on the composition convention
questions.why: A 4-cycle has sign (−1)³ = −1 and a 3-cycle has sign (−1)² = +1, so the product is −1. Sign is a homomorphism into {±1}, so 0 is impossible, and the sign of a permutation does not depend on how products are written.

questions.q: How many elements of S₅ are conjugate to (1 2)(3 4)?
questions.why: Count double transpositions: choose the fixed point (5 ways), then split the remaining 4 points into 2 pairs (3 ways): 15. Equivalently 5!/(2² × 2! × 1) = 120/8 = 15. 10 is the number of transpositions, 20 the number of 3-cycles, and 30 the number of 4-cycles.

questions.q: Determine the conjugacy classes of A₅ and their sizes, and deduce that A₅ is simple.
markScheme: Lists the even cycle types in S₅: e, (2,2,1), (3,1,1), (5)
Sizes in S₅: 1, 15, 20, 24
Explains that 3-cycles and double transpositions do not split (they commute with an odd permutation, e.g. a disjoint transposition or one of their own transpositions)
Explains that 5-cycles split into 12 + 12 (centraliser in S₅ is ⟨σ⟩ ⊆ A₅)
Normal subgroup is union of classes including 1, order dividing 60; checks only 1 and 60 possible
questions.modelAnswer: Even permutations in S₅ have cycle types e, (2,2,1), (3,1,1) and (5), with S₅-class sizes 1, 5!/(2²·2!) = 15, 5!/(3·2!) = 20 and 5!/5 = 24. An S₅-class stays a single A₅-class if some odd permutation commutes with σ. (1 2 3) commutes with the odd (4 5), so the 20 3-cycles form one A₅-class. (1 2)(3 4) commutes with the odd (1 2), so the 15 double transpositions form one class. For σ = (1 2 3 4 5), |C_S₅(σ)| = 120/24 = 5, so C_S₅(σ) = ⟨σ⟩ ⊆ A₅; hence the class splits into two A₅-classes of 12. So A₅ has classes of sizes 1, 15, 20, 12, 12. A normal subgroup N is a union of classes containing {e}, with |N| dividing 60. The possible sums are 1, 13, 16, 21, 25, 28, 33, 36, 40, 45, 48, 60, and only 1 and 60 divide 60. So N = {e} or A₅, and A₅ is simple.

questions.q:
(a) Let a finite group G act on a set X. Define the orbit and stabiliser of x ∈ X and prove the orbit–stabiliser theorem. [7]
(b) Let G be the group of rotations of a cube. Use (a) to show |G| = 24. [4]
(c) By considering the action of G on the four long diagonals of the cube, prove that G ≅ S₄. [9]
markScheme: (a) Correct definitions; Stab(x) shown to be a subgroup
(a) Map g Stab(x) ↦ g·x shown well defined and injective via g·x = h·x ⇔ h⁻¹g ∈ Stab(x)
(a) Surjective onto Orb(x); Lagrange gives |G| = |Orb(x)||Stab(x)|
(b) Transitive on 6 faces, face stabiliser of order 4, so |G| = 24
(c) Action gives homomorphism φ: G → S₄
(c) Kernel: a rotation fixing every diagonal as a line; a non-identity rotation fixes only its axis and, if a half-turn, lines perpendicular to it
(c) At least three diagonals would lie in one plane, but any three are linearly independent; so ker φ trivial
(c) φ injective and |G| = |S₄| = 24, so φ is an isomorphism
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Orb(x) = {g·x : g ∈ G} and Stab(x) = {g ∈ G : g·x = x}. Stab(x) is a subgroup: e·x = x; if g, h fix x then (gh)·x = g·(h·x) = x, and g⁻¹·x = g⁻¹·(g·x) = x. Define θ from left cosets of S = Stab(x) to Orb(x) by θ(gS) = g·x. For g, h ∈ G, g·x = h·x ⇔ (h⁻¹g)·x = x ⇔ h⁻¹g ∈ S ⇔ gS = hS. The forward direction shows θ is well defined; the backward direction shows it is injective. It is surjective by definition of the orbit. So |Orb(x)| equals the number of left cosets of S, which is |G|/|S| by Lagrange. Hence |G| = |Orb(x)| |Stab(x)|.

(b) G acts on the 6 faces. The quarter-turns about the three face axes move any face to any adjacent face, and two of them move it to the opposite face, so the action is transitive: |Orb| = 6. A rotation fixing the top face also fixes the bottom face and is a rotation about the vertical axis; exactly 4 of these (through 0, π/2, π, 3π/2) preserve the cube. So |G| = 6 × 4 = 24.

(c) Place the cube as [−1, 1]³. Its long diagonals are the lines through 0 in directions d₁ = (1,1,1), d₂ = (1,−1,1), d₃ = (−1,1,1), d₄ = (−1,−1,1). Each rotation of the cube permutes the vertices and fixes the centre, so it permutes the four diagonals, giving a homomorphism φ: G → S₄. Suppose g ∈ ker φ, so g maps each diagonal to itself (possibly reversing it). If g ≠ e it is a rotation through some angle about an axis ℓ. A line through 0 mapped to itself by g is either ℓ or, when g is a half-turn, a line perpendicular to ℓ; for other angles no line other than ℓ is preserved. If g is not a half-turn, at most one diagonal (ℓ itself) is preserved, a contradiction. If g is a half-turn, at most one diagonal equals ℓ, so at least three diagonals lie in the plane perpendicular to ℓ. But any three of d₁, …, d₄ are linearly independent; for example det[d₁; d₂; d₃] = 1(−1 − 1) − 1(1 + 1) + 1(1 − 1) = −4 ≠ 0, and the other triples are similar by symmetry. This is a contradiction, so ker φ = {e} and φ is injective. Since |G| = 24 = |S₄| by (b), φ is a bijection, so G ≅ S₄.

questions.q:
(a) Define a normal subgroup K of a group G and show that G/K is a group under (aK)(bK) = abK. [6]
(b) State and prove the isomorphism theorem for a homomorphism φ: G → H. [6]
(c) Show that the map GL₂(ℂ) → M, A ↦ f_A, where f_A(z) = (az + b)/(cz + d) for A = [[a, b], [c, d]], is a surjective homomorphism, and deduce that the Möbius group M is isomorphic to GL₂(ℂ)/Z, where Z = {λI : λ ∈ ℂ \ {0}}. [8]
markScheme: (a) Definition gKg⁻¹ = K; well-definedness via a'b' = ab(b⁻¹k₁b)k₂
(a) Group axioms in G/K (identity K, inverse a⁻¹K, associativity inherited)
(b) Statement G/ker φ ≅ im φ; ker φ normal
(b) θ(g ker φ) = φ(g) well defined, injective, homomorphism, onto im φ
(c) Checks f_A ∘ f_B = f_AB by composing or matrix multiplication; surjective since every Möbius map has a non-singular coefficient matrix
(c) Kernel: f_A = id forces f_A(0) = 0, f_A(∞) = ∞, f_A(1) = 1, giving b = c = 0, a = d
(c) Kernel = Z; isomorphism theorem gives M ≅ GL₂(ℂ)/Z
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) K ≤ G is normal if gKg⁻¹ = K for every g ∈ G. If aK = a'K and bK = b'K then a' = ak₁, b' = bk₂ with kᵢ ∈ K, and a'b' = ab(b⁻¹k₁b)k₂; normality gives b⁻¹k₁b ∈ K, so a'b'K = abK and the operation is well defined. Associativity: (aK bK)cK = (ab)cK = a(bc)K = aK(bK cK). Identity: eK = K, since aK·K = aK. Inverse: a⁻¹K, since aK a⁻¹K = K. So G/K is a group.

(b) Let φ: G → H be a homomorphism and K = ker φ. Then K ◁ G (if φ(k) = e then φ(gkg⁻¹) = e), and G/K ≅ im φ. Define θ(gK) = φ(g). For g, h ∈ G, gK = hK ⇔ h⁻¹g ∈ K ⇔ φ(h)⁻¹φ(g) = e ⇔ φ(g) = φ(h). Reading left to right shows θ is well defined; right to left shows it is injective. θ(gK hK) = θ(ghK) = φ(g)φ(h) = θ(gK)θ(hK), so θ is a homomorphism, and its image is im φ. Hence θ: G/K → im φ is an isomorphism.

(c) For A = [[a, b], [c, d]] and B = [[p, q], [r, s]], f_A(f_B(z)) = (a(pz + q)/(rz + s) + b)/(c(pz + q)/(rz + s) + d) = ((ap + br)z + (aq + bs))/((cp + dr)z + (cq + ds)) = f_AB(z), with the usual conventions at ∞. So A ↦ f_A is a homomorphism. Every Möbius map has some coefficient matrix with ad − bc ≠ 0, which lies in GL₂(ℂ), so the map is surjective. Kernel: suppose f_A(z) = z for all z. f_A(∞) = ∞ forces c = 0; f_A(0) = b/d = 0 forces b = 0; then f_A(z) = az/d, and f_A(1) = 1 gives a = d. So A = aI with a ≠ 0. Conversely every λI gives the identity map. So the kernel is Z, and by the isomorphism theorem M ≅ GL₂(ℂ)/Z.
